claim: Cnidarians are generally accepted to be the sister group to bilaterians.
source: Cnidarians are generally accepted to be the sister group to bilaterians (Brusca et al., 2016; Erwin et al., 2011; Leclère and Röttinger, 2016; Zapata et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Cnidarians owe most of their contractile power to epitheliomuscular or myoepithelial cells that make up both epithelial body layers.
source: In contrast to bilaterians, cnidarians owe most of their contractile power to epitheliomuscular or myoepithelial cells that make up both epithelial body layers (Brusca et al., 2016; Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Epitheliomuscular cells contain interconnected contractile basal extensions (myonemes or myofilaments) that form longitudinal or circular sheets.
source: These specialized cells contain interconnected contractile basal extensions (myonemes or myofilaments) that altogether form longitudinal or circular sheets and play a role equivalent to the muscle layers of other animals.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about cnidarian cell structure

claim: Epitheliomuscular cells are connected to nerve cells via chemical synapses.
source: Epitheliomuscular cells are connected to nerve cells via chemical synapses (Westfall et al., 1971).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In medusae, locomotion is achieved by the rhythmic pulsation of circular sheets of epithelial striated muscles located around the bell margins and lining the subumbrellar surface.
source: In medusae, locomotion is achieved by the rhythmic pulsation of circular sheets of epithelial striated muscles located around the bell margins and lining the subumbrellar surface.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about medusa locomotion

claim: Muscle contractions in medusae are counteracted by the elastic properties and antagonistic force of the mesoglea and result in expulsion of water from beneath the bell.
source: These contractions are counteracted by the elastic properties and antagonistic force of the mesoglea and result in expulsion of water from beneath the bell and thus displacement of the medusa via jet propulsion (Brusca et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Haootia quadriformis from the Ediacaran (ca. 560 Ma) roughly resembles modern stalked jellyfish.
source: Haootia quadriformis from the Ediacaran (Fermeuse Formation; ca. 560 Ma; Newfoundland, eastern Canada) roughly resembles modern stalked jellyfish, such as staurozoans, and bears very fine wrinkles interpreted as putative coronal muscles (Liu et al., 2014a; Liu et al., 2015; see also Miranda et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Haootia quadriformis bears very fine wrinkles interpreted as putative coronal muscles.
source: Haootia quadriformis from the Ediacaran (Fermeuse Formation; ca. 560 Ma; Newfoundland, eastern Canada) roughly resembles modern stalked jellyfish, such as staurozoans, and bears very fine wrinkles interpreted as putative coronal muscles (Liu et al., 2014a; Liu et al., 2015; see also Miranda et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Conulariids have been resolved as stem-group Scyphozoa.
source: Conulariids have been resolved as stem-group Scyphozoa (Van Iten et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Yunnanoascus haikouensis from the early Cambrian Chengjiang Lagerstätte (ca. 521 Ma) shares morphological features with modern jellyfish.
source: Convincing evidence for ancestral jellyfish-like medusozoans comes from the early Cambrian Chengjiang Lagerstätte (ca. 521 Ma; Yunnan Province China) and is best exemplified by Yunnanoascus haikouensis, which shares a set of morphological features with modern jellyfish such as a tetramerous symmetry, rhopalia, long tentacles around the bell margin, and a possible manubrium in the central part of the bell (Han et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: No trace of possible coronal muscles can be seen in Yunnanoascus from the Chengjiang Lagerstätte.
source: Although Chengjiang fossils usually show extremely fine details of soft animal tissues and organs (including digestive, nervous, and reproductive systems), muscles remain elusive, and no trace of possible coronal muscles can be seen in Yunnanoascus.
evidence: Based on observation of fossil specimens

claim: Jellyfish from the mid-Cambrian Marjum Formation (ca. 505 Ma) display relatively well-preserved coronal muscles that suggest swimming capacities.
source: Other jellyfish from the mid-Cambrian Marjum Formation (ca. 505 Ma, Utah, USA; see Cartwright et al., 2007) display fine recognizable anatomical details such as the exumbrella and subumbrella, tentacles and relatively well-preserved coronal muscles that suggest swimming capacities.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The Kuanchuanpu Formation is approximately 535 Ma old.
source: The Kuanchuanpu Formation (ca. 535 Ma, lowermost Cambrian Fortunian Stage; Shaanxi Province, south China)
evidence: Based on radiochronology data cited in Materials and methods

claim: Post-embryonic Olivooides has anatomical features typical of modern cnidarians including radial symmetry, single body opening, exumbrella and subumbrella, interradial septa, gonads, manubrium, oral lips, apertural lobes, tentacles, frenula and velaria.
source: However, microtomography clearly shows that post-embryonic Olivooides does have anatomical features typical of modern cnidarians, a radial symmetry, single body opening, exumbrella and subumbrella, interradial septa (internal ridges), gonads, manubrium, oral lips, apertural lobes, tentacles, frenula and velaria (Dong et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2016; Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The anatomical features of Olivooides support its placement within Medusozoa.
source: which collectively support its placement and that of related forms within Medusozoa (Dong et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2016; Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2016b; Liu et al., 2014b; Liu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The 12 fossil specimens studied have diagnostic features of post-embryonic olivooids including an ovoid shape, pentaradial symmetry and the presence of a periderm, apertural lobes, exumbrella, perradial ridges, and interradial furrows.
source: The 12 fossil specimens studied here have the diagnostic features of post-embryonic olivooids (Dong et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2016; Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020), such as an ovoid shape, pentaradial symmetry and the presence of a periderm, apertural lobes, exumbrella, perradial ridges, and interradial furrows (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2; Figure 2A-E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and references to figures showing specimen morphology

claim: The fossil specimens display a well-preserved network of circular fibers.
source: They also display a well-preserved network of circular fibers (Figures 1 and 2A–E), tentatively interpreted as coronal muscles by Wang et al., 2017 in a pilot study.
evidence: Supported by observation of fossil specimens shown in figures

claim: The body of the studied specimens has a consistent ovoid shape and size with diameter between 560 and 580 μm.
source: The body has a consistent ovoid shape and size (diameter between 560 and 580 μm)
evidence: Based on measurements of fossil specimens

claim: The body is enclosed by a smooth periderm 5–10 μm in thickness.
source: and is enclosed by a smooth periderm (5–10 μm in thickness) (Figure 1—figure supplement Figure 1—figure supplements 1A and 2C, E-H).
evidence: Based on measurements and observations shown in figures

claim: Circular fibers are best developed around the oral aperture where they form four or five separate concentric bundles with individual thickness between 9 and 15 µm.
source: The partial loss of the periderm and perradial apertural lobes in numerous specimens reveals a fine network of underlying closely packed, circular fibers, that are best developed around the oral aperture where they form four or five separate concentric bundles (individual thickness between 9 and 15 µm), each consisting of numerous (possibly up to eight) individual fibers (Figures 1B,C,2B,C,E and F).
evidence: Based on measurements and observations shown in figures

claim: Individual fibers are cylindrical with diameter ca. 2 µm.
source: Individual fibers are cylindrical (diameter ca. 2 µm), lying mostly parallel to each other, although oblique V-shaped interconnections (angle ca. 20–30°) may occur locally (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on measurements and observations shown in figures

claim: Fibers are finely and evenly coated with microcrystalline (ca 0.4 µm) calcium phosphate.
source: Fibers are finely and evenly coated with microcrystalline (ca 0.4 µm) calcium phosphate (Figure 1B, C and E).
evidence: Based on observations shown in figures

claim: Circular fibers clearly extend into the triangular perradial apertural lobes.
source: Circular fibers clearly extend into the triangular perradial apertural lobes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, E, F; Figure 2A and D).
evidence: Based on observations shown in figures

claim: The close-knit circular fibers found in the bell of Olivooidae sp. can be confidently interpreted as epithelial muscle fibers.
source: The close-knit circular fibers found in the bell of Olivooidae sp. can be confidently interpreted as epithelial muscle fibers based on their individual cylindrical shape, size range (around 2 µm in diameter), regular arrangement in bundles (e.g. possibly five more around the bell margin), and closely-packed distribution over a single anatomical surface corresponding to the subumbrella (Figure 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on inference from morphological characteristics and comparison with modern cnidarians

claim: The interpretation of circular fibers as muscle fibers is strongly supported by close similarities with the muscular system of modern cnidarians.
source: Our interpretation is also strongly supported by close similarities with the muscular system of modern cnidarians (myoepithelial cells; MEC).
evidence: Based on comparison with modern cnidarians

claim: The medusae of hydrozoans display a continuous network of circular striated and radial smooth muscles covering the underside of their bell (subumbrella).
source: For example, the medusae of hydrozoans (Figure 2G–I; Figure 3A) display a continuous network of circular striated and radial smooth muscles covering the underside of their bell (subumbrella).
evidence: Based on observations of modern hydrozoans shown in figures

claim: Individual muscle fibers in hydrozoan medusae are 1-to-4-µm-thick and show oblique interconnections.
source: These 1-to-4-µm-thick individual fibers show oblique interconnections (Figure 2G-I; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and sparser radial smooth fibers run perpendicular to them (Leclère and Röttinger, 2016).
evidence: Based on observations and citation to published literature

claim: A very similar configuration to modern hydrozoans can be seen in early Cambrian olivooids.
source: A very similar configuration can be seen in early Cambrian olivooids, which display continuous circular fibers (in some cases covered by transversal structures imprinted on the circular bundles; see Figures 1—3).
evidence: Based on comparison between fossil and modern specimens

claim: Microscopic series of functional units (sarcomeres) that characterize striated muscles are not discernible in the muscle network of Cambrian olivooids.
source: Microscopic series of functional units (sarcomeres) that characterize striated muscles and give them a typical striated appearance (Figure 2G-I; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) are not discernible in the muscle network of Cambrian olivooids, making it impossible to class them as striated or smooth (Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2007).
evidence: Based on observation of fossil specimens

claim: The muscles of olivooids seem to be more developed and concentrated around the bell margin, as seen in modern jellyfish.
source: The muscles of olivooids seem to be more developed and concentrated around the bell margin, as seen in modern jellyfish, such as Clytia, Pelagia, and Chrysaora (Figure 2G-I; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on comparison between fossil and modern specimens

claim: The muscle fibers of olivooids distribute over a surface interpreted as the inner layer of the bell (subumbrella), as in modern medusae.
source: The muscle fibers of olivooids distribute over a surface interpreted as the inner layer of the bell (subumbrella), as in modern medusae.
evidence: Based on comparison with modern medusae

claim: Modern cnidarians have myoepithelial cells that are fully integrated into the ectodermal and endodermal epithelial tissues.
source: In contrast with the distinct muscle system of bilaterians, modern cnidarians have myoepithelial cells that are fully integrated into the ectodermal and endodermal epithelial tissues.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about cnidarian anatomy

claim: The muscular system of Cambrian olivooids was similarly composed of myoepithelial cells that had myofilaments projecting from their basal side.
source: Although the cellular organization cannot be seen in the present fossil material, we hypothesize that the muscular system of Cambrian olivooids was similarly composed of myoepithelial cells that had myofilaments projecting from their basal side.
evidence: Based on speculation and comparison with modern cnidarians

claim: The circular network of olivooids may have been supplemented by longitudinal muscles accommodated within adradial furrows.
source: The circular network of olivooids may have been supplemented by longitudinal muscles accommodated within adradial furrows (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on speculation about fossil anatomy

claim: No clear individual fibers could be distinguished in adradial areas possibly owing to decay or taphonomy.
source: However, no clear individual fibers could be distinguished in these adradial areas possibly owing to decay or taphonomy.
evidence: Based on observation and speculation about preservation

claim: The close-knit fibrous network described in post-embryonic olivooids is the oldest record of a muscular system in cnidarians and more generally in animals.
source: In summary, the close-knit fibrous network described here in post-embryonic olivooids is the oldest record of a muscular system in cnidarians and more generally in animals.
evidence: Based on comparison with other fossil records and the age of the Kuanchuanpu Formation

claim: The occurrence of strong muscles around the bell aperture and inside the perradial apertural lappets suggests that olivooids could contract their bell as modern medusae do.
source: The occurrence of strong muscles around the bell aperture and inside the perradial apertural lappets suggests that olivooids could contract their bell as modern medusae do (Figures 3A–C ,–4A–C).
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical observations

claim: In extant jellyfish, muscle contractions are counteracted by the elastic properties and antagonistic force of the adjacent mesoglea.
source: In extant jellyfish, these contractions are counteracted by the elastic properties and antagonistic force of the adjacent mesoglea.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about jellyfish locomotion

claim: Olivooids are distinguished by an unusual pentaradial symmetry and life cycle with an ovoid post-embryonic stage developing into a conical polyp.
source: Although olivooids share important external and internal morphological features with medusozoans (Dong et al., 2013; Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020), they are distinguished by an unusual pentaradial symmetry and life cycle (with an ovoid post-embryonic stage developing into a conical polyp).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The life cycle of olivooids has no direct counterpart in modern medusozoans.
source: This life cycle has no direct counterpart in modern medusozoans (e.g. Brusca et al., 2016) that develop from a motile planula larva into a polyp and eventually a juvenile medusa through various processes (e.g. strobilation generating ephyrae in scyphozoans; see Gershwin, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The post-embryonic stage of olivooids combined the characters of a medusa with those of a polyp.
source: It has been suggested (Wang et al., 2020) that the post-embryonic stage of olivooids combined the characters of a medusa with those of a polyp and thus would resemble a juvenile sessile jellyfish almost encased within a periderm, with its bell aperture facing upwards.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The movement of olivooids was most probably strongly hindered by its periderm.
source: Whereas the movement of modern medusae is unconstrained, that of olivooids was most probably strongly hindered by its periderm (Bengtson and Yue, 1997; Steiner et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference and citations to published literature

claim: The assumed mesoglea layer of olivooids seems to have been very thin, thus limiting its dynamic capacity.
source: The assumed mesoglea layer of olivooids seems to have been very thin (narrow gap between ex- and subumbrella; see Han et al., 2013; Han et al., 2016b; Dong et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020) thus limiting its dynamic capacity.
evidence: Based on inference from observations and citations to published literature

claim: Swimming efficiency of modern medusae depends on the power and distribution of muscles but also largely on the flexibility of the bell margin.
source: Swimming efficiency of modern medusae depends on the power and distribution of muscles but also largely on the flexibility of the bell margin, a condition that is not found in olivooids.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about medusa locomotion

claim: Powerful muscle contractions in olivooids may have been able to propel the animal over a very short distance but are unlikely to have sustained dynamic locomotion through the water column.
source: Powerful muscle contractions may have been able to propel the animal over a very short distance but are unlikely to have sustained dynamic locomotion through the water column.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical constraints

claim: Feeding in post-embryonic olivooids may have been achieved by rhythmic contractions of their circular muscles, especially those bordering the bell aperture.
source: Feeding may have been achieved by a different method, such as the rhythmic contractions of their circular muscles, especially those bordering the bell aperture (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Based on speculation about function

claim: Such contractions may have resulted in pumping and engulfing sea water containing potential food particles.
source: Such contractions may have resulted in pumping and engulfing sea water containing potential food particles.
evidence: Based on speculation about function

claim: Extant jellyfish such as Aurelia feed by a comparable mechanism.
source: Extant jellyfish such as Aurelia feed by a comparable mechanism (Costello and Colin, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The origin of medusae swimming, associated with the loss of periderm, is an exaptation of rhythmic feeding and respiration among benthic periderm-dwelling medusozoans, probably during Ediacarian-Cambrian period.
source: In this context, we could make the bold speculation that the origin of medusae swimming, associated with the subsequent loss of periderm, is an exaptation of rhythmic feeding and respiration among benthic periderm-dwelling medusozoans, probably during Ediacarian-Cambrian period (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Explicitly stated as speculation

claim: The shift of the actin-myosin system from strictly intracellular to intercellular functions seems to have occurred in the early stages of metazoan evolution.
source: The shift of the actin-myosin system from strictly intracellular to intercellular functions seems to have occurred in the early stages of metazoan evolution (Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Sponges have myocytes around the osculum that play a role in expelling wastes.
source: For example, sponges have myocytes around the osculum that play a role in expelling wastes (Bagby, 1966).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fiber cells of placozoans such as Trichoplax adherens have contractile extensions packed with actin filaments that link the ventral and dorsal epithelia.
source: The fiber cells of placozoans such as Trichoplax adherens have contractile extensions packed with actin filaments that link the ventral and dorsal epithelia (Armon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The gliding motility of placozoans is mainly performed by ciliated epithelial cells.
source: Although the gliding motility of placozoans is mainly performed by ciliated epithelial cells, fiber cells seem to be involved in active body deformation and invagination possibly related to feeding (Smith and Mayorova, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The integration of the actin-myosin system within a dense network of myoepithelial cells as seen in Cambrian and modern cnidarians is likely to have been a major innovation that provided animals with new capacities for powerful movements.
source: The integration of the actin-myosin system within a dense network of myoepithelial cells as seen in Cambrian and modern cnidarians is likely to have been a major innovation that provided animals with new capacities for powerful movements (e.g. swimming, feeding, respiration, etc.).
evidence: Based on inference from evolutionary context

claim: The myoepithelial fiber network seen in post-embryonic olivooids may represent one of the oldest and basic types of animal muscle systems that probably has its origin in the late Precambrian.
source: We suggest that the myoepithelial fiber network seen in post-embryonic olivooids may represent one of the oldest and basic types of animal muscle systems that probably has its origin in the late Precambrian.
evidence: Based on inference from fossil age and evolutionary context

claim: Larger jellyfish from the early and mid-Cambrian are likely to have co-opted the basic muscle system for more diverse functions such as swimming within the water column and prey capture.
source: Larger jellyfish from the early (e.g. Han et al., 2016a) and mid-Cambrian (Marjum Lagerstätte; coronal muscles, Cartwright et al., 2007) are likely to have co-opted this basic system for more diverse functions such as swimming within the water column (e.g. active jet propulsion) and prey capture as seen in modern jellyfish such as Aurelia.
evidence: Based on inference and citations to published literature

claim: Modern representatives of scalidophoran worms such as Priapulus have a close-knit network of circular and longitudinal muscle lining the inner surface of the body wall.
source: Modern representatives of the group such as Priapulus have a close-knit network of circular and longitudinal muscle lining the inner surface of the body wall, that is surrounded by ECM (Figure 4D, F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and often termed 'Hautmuskelschlauch' (HMS; see Schmidt-Rhaesa, 2007).
evidence: Supported by observations and citation to published literature

claim: The enclosed mass of incompressible fluid (hydroskeleton) that fills the primary cavity of scalidophoran worms is the principal antagonist for muscular action.
source: The enclosed mass of incompressible fluid (hydroskeleton) that fills the primary cavity of such worms is the principal antagonist for muscular action (Figure 4).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about worm locomotion

claim: Dynamic interactions between HMS and hydroskeleton allow scalidophoran worms to perform repeated body contraction and extension for burrowing and feeding.
source: Dynamic interactions between HMS and hydroskeleton allow them to perform repeated body contraction and extension for burrowing (Figure 4D–F) (e.g. Vannier et al., 2010) and feeding.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Based on anatomical and functional similarities with modern priapulids, Cambrian scalidophorans also had a HMS-type musculature and possible retractors.
source: Based on remarkable anatomical and functional similarities with modern priapulids (Figure 4D, F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we posit that Cambrian scalidophorans also had a HMS-type musculature and possible retractors.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison with modern organisms

claim: Abundant crawling and burrowing traces found in the basal Cambrian and late Precambrian could not have been made without the action of HMS on a hydrostatic skeleton.
source: This hypothesis is supported by abundant crawling and burrowing traces found in the basal Cambrian (e.g. treptichnid burrow systems; see Kesidis et al., 2019; Vannier et al., 2010) and the late Precambrian (e.g. Evans et al., 2020; Gehling et al., 2001) that could not have been made without the action of HMS on a hydrostatic skeleton (Figure 4D, F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and inference

claim: HMS clearly differs from the musculature of olivooid cnidarians in that HMS does not consist of myoepithelial cells and the antagonist is not the mesoglea but the primary cavity filled with fluid.
source: HMS clearly differs from the musculature of olivooid cnidarians in at least two key features: (1) HMS does not consist of myoepithelial cells and (2) the antagonist onto which muscular force transferred is not the mesoglea but the primary cavity filled with fluid (Leclère and Röttinger, 2016).
evidence: Based on comparison and citation to published literature

claim: Lobopodians is an informal group of ecdysozoans with an annulated cuticle and paired soft legs (lobopods).
source: Lobopodians (e.g. Ortega-Hernández, 2015) is an informal group of ecdysozoans with an annulated cuticle and paired soft legs (lobopods), that is crucial for understanding the remote ancestry of euarthropods.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Most recent phylogenetic trees have resolved Cambrian lobopodians as an 'intermediate' group between scalidophoran worms and arthropods with an arthropodized exoskeleton.
source: Most recent phylogenetic trees (e.g. Aria et al., 2021; Giribet and Edgecombe, 2019) have resolved Cambrian lobopodians as an 'intermediate' group between scalidophoran worms and arthropods with an arthropodized exoskeleton.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The inner surface of the body wall of lobopodians was lined with closely packed circular and longitudinal muscle fibers that seem to have extended into the limbs.
source: The inner surface of their body wall was lined with closely packed circular and longitudinal muscle fibers that seem to have extended into the limbs (see Tritonychus in Zhang et al., 2016; Figure 4G, H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and reference to figures

claim: In Paucipodia from the Chengjiang Lagerstätte, a connecting strand runs between the terminal claw of the limbs and the area surrounding the gut and is interpreted as a possible retractor muscle.
source: In Paucipodia from the Chengjiang Lagerstätte (see Vannier and Martin, 2017; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-E), a connecting strand runs between the terminal claw of the limbs and the area surrounding the gut and is interpreted here as a possible retractor muscle (see analogues in extant onychophorans De Sena Oliveira and Mayer, 2013).
evidence: Based on observation and inference supported by citation

claim: Larger Cambrian lobopodians such as Pambdelurion from the Sirius Passet Lagerstätte are characterized by a more complex musculature with paired, lateral, ventral and dorsal longitudinal muscles.
source: Although unsegmented as in smaller lobopodians, larger Cambrian lobopodians such as Pambdelurion from the Sirius Passet Lagerstätte (ca. 520 Ma) are characterized by a more complex musculature with paired, lateral, ventral and dorsal longitudinal muscles.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about Pambdelurion

claim: Well-developed bundles of extrinsic and intrinsic limb muscles presumably controlled leg motion in larger Cambrian lobopodians as in modern onychophorans.
source: Well-developed bundles of extrinsic and intrinsic limb muscles presumably controlled their leg motion as in modern onychophorans (Budd, 1998; Hoyle and Williams, 1980; Young and Vinther, 2017; see Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Based on inference and citations to published literature

claim: Early euarthropods had already acquired rigid exoskeletal elements (sclerotized cuticular elements jointed by an arthrodial membrane) that were operated by a lever-like system of segmentally arranged antagonistic muscles.
source: Early euarthropods that co-existed with lobopodians and scalidophoran worms (e.g. Burgess-Shale-type Lagerstätten) had already acquired rigid exoskeletal elements (sclerotized cuticular elements jointed by an arthrodial membrane, such as body sclerites and appendage podomeres) that were operated by a lever-like system of segmentally arranged antagonistic muscles as seen in Kiisortoqia and Camparamuta from the Sirius Passet Lagerstätte (Young and Vinther, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The rise of euarthropods was associated with a profound rearrangement of the muscle system possibly inherited from lobopodian ancestors, such as the reduction of the circular HMS musculature.
source: This suggests that the rise of euarthropods was associated with a profound rearrangement of the muscle system possibly inherited from lobopodian ancestors, such as the reduction of the circular HMS musculature that lost its primary hydrostatic function and peristaltic capabilities because of exoskeletal rigidity (Young and Vinther, 2017).
evidence: Based on inference and citation to published literature

claim: Well-developed sigmoidal blocks occur within the trunk of early and mid-Cambrian chordates such as Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys and Pikaia.
source: Well-developed sigmoidal blocks occur within the trunk of early and mid-Cambrian chordates such as Myllokunmingia (Shu et al., 1996) and Haikouichthys (Shu et al., 2003; possibly craniate) and Pikaia (Conway Morris and Caron, 2012; stem-group chordate).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The sigmoidal blocks in early Cambrian chordates recall the W-shaped wall musculature of modern cephalochordates such as Branchiostoma and fish, which is derived from segmental coelomic compartments.
source: They recall the W-shaped wall musculature of modern cephalochordates such as Branchiostoma and fish, which is derived from segmental coelomic compartments.
evidence: Based on comparison with modern organisms

claim: These assumed muscle blocks occupied much of the body wall of ancient chordates and most probably played a crucial role in swimming.
source: These assumed muscle blocks occupied much of the body wall of these ancient chordates and most probably played a crucial role in swimming.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomy

claim: Different types of musculature co-existed among early Cambrian animals: (1) myoepithelial circular (MEC) muscles in cnidarians, (2) grid-like and subepidermal (HMS) muscles in scalidophoran worms, (3) HMS and extrinsic muscles to control leg motion in lobopodians, (4) segmentally arranged muscles tightly integrated to exoskeletal elements in early euarthropods, (5) well-developed W-shaped muscles in early chordates.
source: In summary, both fossil and indirect evidence presented here indicate that different types of musculature co-existed among early Cambrian animals: (1) myoepithelial circular (MEC) muscles in cnidarians, (2) grid-like and subepidermal (HMS) muscles in scalidophoran worms, (3) HMS and extrinsic muscles to control leg motion in lobopodians, (4) segmentally arranged muscles tightly integrated to exoskeletal elements in early euarthropods, (5) well-developed W-shaped muscles in early chordates.
evidence: Based on synthesis of fossil and comparative evidence

claim: The myoepithelial system appears as the most basic muscle system.
source: Whereas the myoepithelial system appears as the most basic one, that of ecdysozoans seems to have undergone considerable changes and diversification over a relatively short time interval during the early Cambrian.
evidence: Based on inference from evolutionary context

claim: The muscle system of ecdysozoans underwent considerable changes and diversification over a relatively short time interval during the early Cambrian.
source: Whereas the myoepithelial system appears as the most basic one, that of ecdysozoans seems to have undergone considerable changes and diversification over a relatively short time interval during the early Cambrian.
evidence: Based on inference from fossil evidence

claim: The diversity and plasticity of muscle systems allowed a great variety of animals to explore and colonize new environments and can be seen as one of the driving forces of the animal radiation.
source: This remarkable diversity and plasticity of muscle systems allowed a great variety of animals to explore and colonize new environments and can be seen as one of the driving forces of the animal radiation.
evidence: Based on inference from evolutionary context

claim: All studied fossils come from phosphatic limestones collected from the Kuanchuanpu Formation at the Shizhonggou section (Ningqiang County, Shaanxi Province, China).
source: All studied fossils come from phosphatic limestones collected from the Kuanchuanpu Formation at the Shizhonggou section (Ningqiang County, Shaanxi Province, China; see Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Statement of geological provenance

claim: Biostratigraphy indicates that the Kuanchuanpu Formation rocks correspond to the Meishucunian Stage that is the equivalent of the lowermost Cambrian Terreneuvian Stage.
source: Biostratigraphy (Anabarites – Protohertzina – Arthrochities zone; Qian, 1977; Qian, 1999) indicates that these rocks correspond to the Meishucunian Stage that is the equivalent of the lowermost Cambrian Terreneuvian Stage.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Radiochronology confirms that the Kuanchuanpu Formation is approximately 535 Ma.
source: Radiochronology (U-Pb method; Sawaki et al., 2008; Peng et al., 2012) confirms that the Kuanchuanpu Formation is approximately 535 Ma.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Secondarily phosphatized fossils were extracted from rocks via a standard acid digestion in 7% acetic acid.
source: Secondarily phosphatized fossils were extracted from rocks via a standard acid digestion in 7% acetic acid.
evidence: Description of methodology

claim: Twelve specimens of Olivooidae bearing well-preserved muscle fibers were selected for the present study.
source: Twelve specimens of Olivooidae (Cnidaria) bearing well-preserved muscle fibers were selected for the present study and mounted for SEM (FEI Quanta 400 FEG scanning electron microscope at Northwest University, China; Au-coating, high-vacuum).
evidence: Description of study materials and methods

claim: The studied specimens belong to Sinaster petalon, Hanagyroia orientalis and Olivooidae sp.
source: They belong to Sinaster petalon Wang et al., 2017 (ELISN115-39), Hanagyroia orientalis Wang et al., 2020 (ELISN107-470) and Olivooidae sp. (ELISN150-278, ELISN111-54, ELISN052-33, ELISN045-143, ELISN012-16, ELISN061-19, ELISN087-64, ELISN088-48, ELISN087-33 and ELISN098-19).
evidence: Statement of taxonomic identification

claim: Clytia hemisphaerica medusae, Eirene sp. medusae, Chrysaora colorata and Pelagia noctiluca metaephyrae were raised in the laboratory.
source: Two-week-old Clytia hemisphaerica medusae, newly released Eirene sp. medusae, 1-month-old Chrysaora colorata and Pelagia noctiluca metaephyrae were raised in the laboratory (Villefranche-sur-mer, France) following Lechable et al., 2020 and Ramondenc et al., 2017 culture protocols.
evidence: Description of methodology supported by citations

claim: Fixation followed by Phalloidin (actin) and Hoechst (nuclei) staining was performed on four jellyfish species.
source: Fixation followed by Phalloidin (actin) and Hoechst (nuclei) staining was performed on the four species as described for Clytia hemisphaerica in Sinigaglia et al., 2020.
evidence: Description of methodology supported by citation

claim: Extant priapulid worms (Priapulus caudatus) were collected from near the Kristineberg Marine Station (Sweden).
source: Extant priapulid worms (Priapulus caudatus) (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1) were collected (JV) from near the Kristineberg Marine Station (Sweden), fixed with glutaraldehyde and dried (Critical Point) for SEM observations (Univ. Lyon).
evidence: Description of methodology
